subtype: Family member in a medical emergency [Actor]
passage:
Harsha,
You asked on the phone why you were the fifth person I called on Sunday, not the first. Here is the honest answer.
Abbu went grey and sank down right there by the tomato cart. My head filled with fifty things at once: which hospital, is there cash in my bag, where is his insurance card, should I ring you, Phuppo, Dr Qureshi? I actually had your number on the screen. Then I remembered the poster from college: call the emergency number first, everything else later. So I dialled 108. The operator asked if he was breathing, told me what to do and to stay with him. The vegetable seller held an umbrella over us. Only when the siren came did I call you, then Phuppo, then the others.
The doctors say getting him in quickly made a difference. I'm sorry you heard it fifth. I'd do it the same way again.
Hafsa

qa.q: Where did Abbu collapse?
qa.a: Right there by the tomato cart.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling when Abbu sank down?
qa.a: Hafsa was panicking, with fifty questions about the hospital, cash, the insurance card and whom to ring all crowding in at once.

qa.q: Why was dialling 108 first the right order?
qa.a: It got help moving straight away and brought the operator's instructions; calls to family and sorting out the hospital could wait until the ambulance came.

qa.q: How might Harsha have felt hearing the news fifth?
qa.a: Harsha was probably hurt and a little left out at first, but the letter may help Harsha see the order was about getting Abbu help fast, not about caring less.

grounding: Shows an adult whose parent collapses, flooded with decisions about hospital, money and relatives, who calls emergency services first and sorts the rest later.

passage:
Friday: Sumit slipped off the ladder while hanging festival lights in the building compound and landed hard, a cut above his eyebrow bleeding into his eye. Neighbours crowded round. "It's nothing, it's nothing, you're fine!" said three voices at once, which frightened him more. Then Ira knelt beside him. "Sumit, you've cut your forehead. It's bleeding, and I'm pressing a clean cloth on it. The ambulance is on its way. I'm staying right here." His breathing slowed.
Saturday: In the ward he hated needing help to reach the toilet and apologised to every nurse. One nurse said, "Now I'm checking your eyes with a light. Now the stitches." Knowing each step made it easier to lie still.
Tuesday: Sumit brought Ira a box of sweets. "When everyone said it was nothing, I thought it must be terrible. When you told me exactly what was happening, I could breathe."

qa.q: What was Sumit doing when he slipped off the ladder?
qa.a: He was hanging festival lights in the building compound.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel in the ward on Saturday?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and dependent, hating to need help to reach the toilet and apologising to every nurse.

qa.q: What could the neighbours learn from Ira?
qa.a: Instead of saying "it's nothing", they could calmly say what has happened, what is being done and that help is coming.

qa.q: How might Ira have felt kneeling beside Sumit while the crowd kept talking?
qa.a: Ira was probably worried but chose to stay calm and clear, focusing on the cloth and the plain facts to keep him steady.

grounding: Shows an injured person who feels frightened, embarrassed and dependent, and is steadied more by a calm voice explaining what is happening than by empty reassurance.

passage: In the Vancouver flat, Xin built a blanket fort and wanted it to glow like a cave. She took a leftover birthday candle and the long lighter from the kitchen drawer, and set the flame on a saucer by her pillow. Then her dog pushed in, and the blanket sagged low over it. Santiago, her stepfather, smelt something hot and pulled the blanket back. The edge had a brown scorch mark. He blew out the candle. "I was watching it the whole time!" Xin said, her lip shaking. "I know you were," he said. "But you didn't see Pepper move the blanket. New rule: candles and lighters only at the kitchen table, with a grown-up. The lighter lives on the top shelf now." Xin stared at the brown mark.

qa.q: Where did Xin put the candle?
qa.a: On a saucer by her pillow.

qa.q: What was Xin feeling when Santiago pulled the blanket back?
qa.a: She was upset and defensive, insisting she was watching it, with her lip shaking, probably also scared by the scorch mark.

qa.q: What did Santiago do that fits a child of Xin's age?
qa.a: He stayed calm, explained the part she couldn't foresee, the dog moving the blanket, and set a clear rule and moved the lighter out of reach.

qa.q: How might Santiago have felt when he smelt something hot?
qa.a: He was probably frightened, but he sat down and spoke gently instead of shouting.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild who plays with fire without imagining what could go wrong, and an adult who responds with a clear rule and limits.

passage: Looking back, I knew exactly how stupid it was while I was doing it. I'm Vaibhav. It was Lohri, and the bonfire in our society compound was taller than me. The older boys were jumping over the edge where the flames were lowest. Jasleen had her phone up. "Vaibhav, your turn! Everyone's watching!" I could feel the heat on my face from two metres away. One voice in my head said, this is how people get burnt. A louder feeling said, if you back out now, you'll be the one who backed out, forever. I ran and jumped. I cleared it, just, but landed badly and turned my ankle. The hem of my kurta smelt of smoke. Chachi threw water on the edge and made everyone stand well back. The video got forty likes. My ankle took weeks to heal. I remember the likes feeling bigger than the ankle, and that's the part that scares me now.

qa.q: How many likes did the video get?
qa.a: Forty likes.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling just before the jump?
qa.a: Vaibhav was scared of getting burnt but more afraid of being seen as the one who backed out, so the fear of losing face won.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav say next time a dare like this comes up?
qa.a: Something short like "Not doing that one, I'll film", and step away towards an adult, since backing out once costs far less than an injury.

qa.q: How might Jasleen have seen the jump while filming?
qa.a: Jasleen was probably excited and caught up in the crowd's cheering, focused on the video rather than on how close the flames were.

grounding: Shows a teenager who attempts a dangerous dare in front of friends, aware of the risk but pulled more strongly by approval.

subtype: Road and vehicle safety in India [Actor]
passage: After Saturday practice at the district football club, Kishore's friends crowded round one scooter in the club car park. Rohit started it, Faizan climbed on behind, and they both looked at Kishore. "Come on, squeeze in. It's two kilometres." Nobody had a helmet. Half the car park rode like this; the watchman didn't even look up. Kishore's hand was already on the seat. Then he pictured the flyover and the trucks. "I'll take the bus," he said. Faizan rolled his eyes. "Seriously? You sound like my mother." Rohit snapped, "We waited for you, yaar." Kishore's face burned, but he stepped back. Coach Elizabeth, locking the kit room, had heard. "Kishore, I'm going your way. Front seat's free." In the car he stared out of the window, still embarrassed. A few minutes later they passed the scooter, wobbling round a pothole with three heads and no helmets.

qa.q: Who was locking the kit room?
qa.a: Coach Elizabeth.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel after saying he'd take the bus?
qa.a: He was embarrassed, his face burning at the teasing, even though he stood by his choice.

qa.q: What made Kishore's choice take courage?
qa.a: Riding three to a scooter without helmets looked normal to everyone, so saying no meant being mocked by friends who were annoyed they had waited.

qa.q: How did Rohit and Faizan see Kishore's refusal?
qa.a: They saw it as fussy and a letdown, rolling their eyes and snapping, because the risk felt ordinary to them.

grounding: Shows a teenager tempted to ride three to a scooter without a helmet because everyone does, and choosing safety against the crowd.

passage: The overnight bus to Goa stopped at a highway dhaba near Kolhapur at midnight, rain dripping off the tin roof, and Salma's phone was down to ten percent. Kunal, from the seat across the aisle, had been chatty since Pune. Now he appeared beside her at the tea counter. "This bus will crawl. My friend's car is outside. Come, you'll reach by six." He asked which hotel she had booked, and when she didn't answer, he asked again. But the back of her neck prickled, and she noticed he was standing between her and the bus. A polite voice in her head said, don't be rude, he's only offering. "No, thanks," she said, and walked, not ran, to the family from row four and stood with them. She quietly told the conductor the man in 12C was bothering her. With her last battery, she messaged her cousin the bus number and her seat. The conductor moved her to the front.

qa.q: How much charge was left on Salma's phone at the dhaba?
qa.a: Ten percent.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling at the tea counter?
qa.a: She felt uneasy, with the back of her neck prickling, and torn between being polite and getting away.

qa.q: Which steps made Salma's exit safe and quiet?
qa.a: She said a simple no without explaining, moved to stand with a family, told the conductor, and messaged her cousin the bus number and seat.

qa.q: How might the conductor see Salma's quiet report?
qa.a: The conductor took it seriously enough to move her to the front, suggesting the report seemed reasonable and worth acting on.

grounding: Shows a young woman travelling alone who notices that something feels off and chooses to leave quietly over being polite.

passage: The cable to the milk steamer at the café in Madrid had been wrapped in black tape for as long as Alejandro had worked there. Seven months. Sometimes, when he pushed the jug under the wand, his fingers tingled. "Little kiss from the machine," he joked. Wanjiru, who worked the till, didn't laugh. "That's a shock, Alejandro. Tell Marta." He shrugged. "It's been like this forever. Nothing's happened." Then on a wet Tuesday, with the queue out of the door, there was a crack and a flash under the counter and a smell of burnt plastic. He jumped back, heart hammering. Wanjiru switched off the socket at the wall. The tape had melted into a black lump. That afternoon an electrician replaced the whole cable, and Marta asked quietly, "How long has it been tingling?" Alejandro looked at the floor. "A while."

qa.q: How long had Alejandro worked at the café?
qa.a: Seven months.

qa.q: How did Alejandro feel when Marta asked how long it had been tingling?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and shaken, looking at the floor, knowing the tingles had been a warning he joked away.

qa.q: What should Alejandro have done after the first tingle?
qa.a: Treated it as a warning, stopped using the steamer and told Marta so the cable could be fixed before anything worse happened.

qa.q: How did Wanjiru see the tingling cable?
qa.a: Wanjiru saw it as a real shock and a danger from the start, which is why Wanjiru didn't laugh and acted fast when it sparked.

grounding: Shows an adult who ignores a hazard and its near misses because nothing has gone wrong so far, until it finally fails.

passage: Forty minutes before the chief guest arrived, Nikita, the fest's stage coordinator, stood under the lighting frame with her torch and didn't like what she saw. On the left, two metal clamps were missing, and a length of rope had been tied in their place. The frame dipped slightly towards the crowd barrier, where students were already packing in. Arnab, the lighting vendor, waved from the console. "It's held for three shows this month, madam. Don't worry." Nikita didn't raise her voice. "Arnab, two clamps are missing on the left, it's tied with rope, and it leans over the front row. I can't open the gates like this. Switch off the left bank, we move the barrier back three metres, and your crew fits clamps before the band." He sighed. "The chief guest is coming." "Then let's start now," she said. His crew found the clamps in the van. By the time the band came on, the frame stood straight.

qa.q: What had been tied in place of the missing clamps?
qa.a: A length of rope.

qa.q: How did Nikita seem to feel as Arnab brushed off her concern?
qa.a: She was worried about the frame but stayed calm and firm, not raising her voice.

qa.q: What made Nikita's objection hard to dismiss?
qa.a: She gave exact facts, two missing clamps, rope, a lean over the front row, and a clear fix that kept the show going while the clamps were fitted.

qa.q: How might Arnab have seen the request?
qa.a: Arnab was probably annoyed and pressed for time with the chief guest coming, and felt his three safe shows proved the frame was fine.

grounding: Illustrates a worker calmly refusing an unsafe setup, giving specific facts and a practical fix under time pressure.

passage: Marek pushed the stool to the kitchen sink in their Kraków flat. "I wash the potatoes!" His dad, Alejandro, handed him the brush and five muddy potatoes. Marek scrubbed each one very hard, tongue poking out. Water splashed on the floor and on the cat. One potato was still brown on one side. Alejandro's hand moved towards it, then stopped. "Good scrubbing. That one has a muddy spot. Can you find it?" Marek turned it round, found the spot and scrubbed again. "All clean!" he shouted, holding it up like a prize. At dinner Marek told everyone, "I made the soup."

qa.q: How many potatoes did Alejandro give Marek?
qa.a: Five muddy potatoes.

qa.q: How did Marek feel holding up the clean potato?
qa.a: Marek felt proud, shouting "All clean!" and holding it up like a prize.

qa.q: What did Alejandro do instead of fixing the potato himself?
qa.a: He praised the scrubbing and asked Marek to find the muddy spot, so Marek could finish the job himself.

qa.q: What was it like for Alejandro to watch the splashing and the brown spot?
qa.a: Alejandro was tempted to take over, since his hand moved towards the potato, but chose patience over a quick, neat job.

grounding: Shows a young child proudly helping with a small kitchen chore, slowly and messily, and a parent who patiently accepts the imperfect help.

subtype: Making own bag, bed and simple food [Actor]
passage: "Sabina, you grumble about making your bed? Sit, let your Dada Lalit tell you. When I was nine, my Ma went to help at my Mama's house for a month, and Dadi said, 'From tomorrow, you do your own mornings.' I had to fold my razai, pack my cloth bag with slate and books, and make tea for the two of us on the stove, with Dadi sitting right there on her stool, watching. The first day I forgot my slate and burnt the milk. Dadi didn't take the pan. She only said, 'Lower the flame, Lalit.' By the second week I could do it all before the school bell. And when Ma came back, I noticed something: how much she did every morning that I had never once seen."

qa.q: What happened on young Lalit's first day of doing his own mornings?
qa.a: He forgot his slate and burnt the milk.

qa.q: How might young Lalit have felt on that first morning?
qa.a: He was probably flustered and embarrassed, with a forgotten slate and burnt milk while Dadi watched.

qa.q: What choice of Dadi's was the turning point for Lalit?
qa.a: Dadi didn't take the pan from him; she only told him to lower the flame, so he kept doing it himself until he could manage alone.

qa.q: How might Ma have felt when she came back after the month?
qa.a: Ma was likely surprised and pleased to find him managing his own mornings, and maybe touched that he now noticed her work.

grounding: Shows a child who learns under supervision to fold bedding, pack a bag and make tea, and comes to see how much housework goes on at home.
